new.n: Murdered strangers' plunder at the blow-hole west of the Ottawa House, Port Sheldon (1840s tale)
new.pl: Ottawa House site, NE shore near the head of Pigeon Lake (Meima 1921 map); the blow-hole and its run lay just W of the hotel
new.v: Plunder from two murdered travellers (no amount)
new.st: An 1874 letter from Gorton L. Scott, left in charge of the Ottawa House after the Port Sheldon land bubble burst, says two strangers who stopped there one October night were murdered by 'Irish Mike' and Dennis, and their bodies and 'some of the plunder' were buried 'near the run at the base of the blow-hole, just west of the hotel'. Scott searched about 1871, but 'shifting sands' had changed the bluffs. Pin is the hotel area, not the spot.
new.t: One 1874 letter; bodies and plunder said buried at a dune blowout W of the hotel; dunes have shifted. Graves: never dig; look only. Private/park land: check ownership. See also 'The receiver's lost gold', the townsite card for the same dead town.
src: Detroit News, 25 Nov 1895, p. 4, "Recalling the Wild Career of a Dead Michigan Town" (West Olive; prints Gorton L. Scott's 1874 letter) (Newspapers.com 1378276826)
Meima, 'A Forgotten City', Michigan History 5 (1921), pp. 408-9 (Ottawa House on the NE shore near the head of Pigeon Lake)
pinev: Ottawa House 'not far from the head of Pigeon Lake', on the NE shore per the old company map (Meima 1921). The lake's head is at about -86.172 on the ArcGIS detailed water-body outline and near -86.162 on 2016 Michigan lidar; the pin sits between, on the N shore, r400 covering both. 1 m lidar tiles for a blowout check W of the hotel are not reachable from here, so no blowout is flagged.

set.t: Single 1921 magazine telling; no period record yet. Shifting dune sand. Township park and private dune lots: permission; the power-plant land is excluded. By 1913 one red building, then a barn, alone remained, and 'the lighthouse and harbor bell are now buried under the shifting sand dunes': the 1830s lighthouse site at the Pigeon Lake entrance lies under the dunes, a sign of how deep the drift is over the townsite. No digs reported. See also the Ottawa House murder-plunder card: the 1895 Detroit News piece on this dead town links other dark deeds to 'the old Scare Valley house'.

1917 Iowa County plat shows no race track
1917 Iowa Co atlas, English Twp plate p. 33 (image 31617_072143-00699): no race track or fairground; town around NE sec 8 / NW sec 9 T78N R11W

Williamsburg Journal-Tribune 1946 'Remember?' column (c.1896 item): Thomas Ingram bought 'the farm upon which the Millersburg race track was located'. 1886 plat: Ingram family land W side sec 16 and NW sec 21 (T78N R11/12W), 1-1.5 mi SE of the village; the track farm Thomas Ingram bought c.1896 is not identified (no 1890s plat in the set); the 1917 directory has no Ingram.
